(using only elementary trigonometric identities) eliminates
the unknown \(x\) and yields

\[
\sin\frac{\theta}{2}= \sin\frac{13\theta}{2}. \tag{6}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Solving for \(\theta\)

Equation (6) gives two possibilities:

* \(\displaystyle\frac{\theta}{2}= \frac{13\theta}{2}+2k\pi\)  
  \(\Rightarrow\displaystyle\theta=-\frac{k\pi}{3}\) – impossible for a
  positive angle.

* \(\displaystyle\frac{\theta}{2}= \pi-\frac{13\theta}{2}+2k\pi\)  
  \(\Rightarrow\displaystyle 7\theta=\pi(1+2k)\).

Since \(\theta\) must satisfy \(0<\theta<\frac{\pi}{3}\)
(\(3\theta\) is the angle at \(A\)), the only admissible integer is
\(k=0\). Hence

\[
\theta=\frac{\pi}{7}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Desired angle

\[
\boxed{\angle BAC=3\theta= \frac{3\pi}{7}}
\qquad\text{(i.e. } \displaystyle \frac{540^\circ}{7}\approx77.14^\circ\text{).}
